bib.title: ALCUNA: Large Language Models Meet New Knowledge
bib.venue: preprint (arXiv v1, 23 Oct 2023); venue not printed in the PDF

read.skipped: reference list skimmed; appendix prompt tables skimmed, filtering and error-analysis appendices read

question: How well do LLMs understand, differentiate and reason with new knowledge that is supplied in the context and is guaranteed not to be in their training data?
contributions: KnowGen: build artificial entities by heredity, variation, extension and dropout over a structured knowledge base
ALCUNA: 84,351 questions about 3,554 artificial organisms from the Encyclopedia of Life
Evaluation of ChatGPT, Alpaca-7B, Vicuna-13B and ChatGLM-6B

method.summary: Generate artificial biological entities from EOL taxonomy data, place their properties in the prompt as structured knowledge, and ask template-generated questions that test understanding (KU), differentiation from the parent entity (KD) and multi-hop association with existing knowledge (KA).
method.task: question answering over in-context new knowledge

datasets.name: ALCUNA
datasets.source: Encyclopedia of Life (2404790 entities, 13625612 properties, 669 property types); questions templated by ChatGPT
datasets.preprocessing: per-model filtering keeps only artificial entities whose parent entities the model recalls perfectly

inference.samples: single pass over the filtered benchmark per setting
inference.prompting: zero-shot and few-shot, vanilla and chain-of-thought ('Let's think step by step'); new knowledge given as structured JSON in the prompt
inference.retrieval: none; the new entity's properties are given directly in the prompt

metrics.name: accuracy
metrics.definition: output matched against the gold answer(s); correct if it matches any of the correct answers

eval.protocol: average per ability (KU, KD, KA); 100 sampled one-hop and 100 multi-hop questions human-checked: 98% and 95% correct

results.claim: ChatGPT reaches 64.37 average accuracy few-shot vanilla but only 41.52 on knowledge association (multi-hop across new and existing knowledge).
results.setup: Few-Shot-Vanilla, filtered ALCUNA, structured (JSON) in-context knowledge
results.table: Table 1, row Avg. and row KA, Few-Shot-Vanilla, column ChatGPT

results.claim: The open models score 35.09 (Alpaca 7B), 42.74 (Vicuna 13B) and 42.56 (ChatGLM 6B) on average few-shot vanilla.
Knowledge association is the hardest ability for all models.
results.setup: all four models, all four prompt settings
results.quote: Among all abilities, knowledge association is obviously the most difficult for LLMs

results.claim: Adding the entities on the reasoning chain to the context lifts KA accuracy (ChatGLM 27.47 to 44.43; Vicuna 30.10 to 33.25), while irrelevant entities lower it (ChatGLM 18.56).
results.table: Table 4, rows artificial, w/ chain, w/ irrelevant

results.claim: Putting the parent entity's knowledge in the context hurts differentiation: ChatGLM falls from 41.42 to 24.71 and Vicuna from 46.76 to 35.04 on KD questions; irrelevant entities cost less.
results.table: Table 3, rows artificial, w/ parent, w/ irrelevant

results.claim: Structured (JSON) input beats natural-language input for all three open models, e.g. ChatGLM average 42.56 vs 20.54.
results.table: Table 5, row Avg., ChatGLM JSON vs NL

results.claim: Models are more confused the more an artificial entity's properties overlap its parent's; only ChatGPT is nearly insensitive.
results.setup: KD questions binned by property similarity, Figure 3
results.quote: The more similar the new entities are to the existing
results.note: Figure 3 read as a plot, no numbers

results.claim: Chain-of-thought and few-shot prompting improve the average in most cases but ChatGPT's CoT does not fix KA (37.88 few-shot CoT vs 41.52 vanilla).
results.table: Table 1, row KA, ChatGPT, Few-Shot-CoT vs Few-Shot-Vanilla

limits: Built on biological taxonomy only (EOL); the authors say other domains are possible but untested.
Only four models, three of them small open models; GPT-4-class models were not evaluated.
Knowledge is given in the prompt in a structured JSON format; the paper measures in-context use of new knowledge, not retrieval, and does not run a retriever.
Questions are template-generated and scored by matching; a 100-question human check found 98% (one-hop) and 95% (multi-hop) correct.
Per-model filtering to entities whose parent was perfectly recalled shrinks the question set differently for each model; comparisons use the intersection.

lineage.note: template questions and recall filtering follow Petroni et al.

lineage.work: Large language models can be easily distracted by irrelevant context
lineage.note: irrelevant context lowers performance, consistent with Shi et al. 2023
